objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain which approaches count as precision for the checkride, choose and brief an ILS, LPV or GLS chart, set up and verify the localizer, glideslope, markers and WAAS, adjust the DA and visibility for category, altimeter source and inoperative parts, teach localizer and glideslope tracking with a descent rate planned for the groundspeed, guard against false glideslopes, teach the decision at the DA, and spot and fix a learner's chart, radio, checklist, flying and DA errors.
why: On a precision approach the obstacle clearance depends on following the vertical guidance, so the learner's job is to stay on the glidepath [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]], and any delay in starting the missed approach at the DA puts the airplane at risk from obstacles in the visual segment [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. A DA is a decision point, not a floor to level off on: if the 91.175(c) conditions are not met there, the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. A false glideslope can lead to a very high descent rate or a pitch-up, possibly with no warning (IFH Addendum B, False Courses, 2019), and chasing the needles without a planned descent rate is a listed ILS error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]] [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. The PTS asks you to teach precise control, sound judgment, low-level wind shear avoidance, checklist use and positive exchange of flight controls [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].

warmup: Think first: in calm air your instrument learner flies the ILS well at 500 fpm. Today, with a 15-knot headwind, the same 500 fpm takes the airplane below the glideslope, and at the DA the learner levels off "to have a look." Why did the old descent rate stop working, and what is wrong with leveling off at a DA?

key_terms.def: An approach whose course and glidepath guidance meet the ICAO Annex 10 precision standards, such as PAR, ILS and GLS [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]. For the CFII checkride it is a standard approach to a published DA using approved vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

A specified altitude, in feet MSL, at which the pilot must decide to continue or to start an immediate missed approach if the required visual reference is not seen [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]]; used on ILS, GLS and vertically guided RNAV approaches [[34:334|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]].
The same decision point expressed as a height in feet above ground [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]]; Category II and III DHs are measured with a radio altimeter [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

The straight-in DA or MDA expressed as height above the touchdown zone elevation [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. A Category I HAT is normally 200 ft; 250 ft or more may come from signal coverage or obstacle penetrations [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

The altitude next to the lightning bolt: the minimum altitude for glideslope interception after a procedure turn [[2:117|Chart Users' Guide p 117]]. Intercepting there marks the start of the final segment [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]].
The planned height of the glideslope antenna over the threshold if the airplane stays on the glidepath; it is not the height where the needle actually centers [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d6]].

Extra glideslope courses at steeper angles, about 6° to 12°, that can look like a normal glideslope or reverse the needle; not met when the charted altitudes are flown and the glideslope is captured from below (IFH Addendum B). False courses and reverse sensing occur at angles well above the published path [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d4]].

An area near the localizer or glideslope antenna where vehicles and aircraft can disturb the signal [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k1]]; with a ceiling of 800 ft or more and 2 miles or more, ATC protects it only on request [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k2(a)]].

A WAAS line of minima with angular lateral and vertical guidance very similar to a Category I ILS, flown to a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]]; the AIM calls it an APV, not a precision approach [[33:102|AIM 1-1-18b1]].
GBAS Landing System: a precision approach using GPS corrected by a ground station at the airport [[33:106|AIM 1-1-19a]], flown with the same technique as an ILS or LPV final [[33:107|AIM 1-1-19f]].

Category I: DH 200 ft and RVR 2,400 (1,800 with touchdown zone and centerline lights, or with autopilot, flight director or HUD); Categories II and III go lower and need special authorization and equipment [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9i1]].

Horizontal visibility along the runway, shown in hundreds of feet, so 24 means 2,400 ft [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. If it is not reported, convert the RVR minimum to ground visibility with the 91.175(h) table [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]].

chunks.title: Which approaches belong to this Task, and choosing the chart

body.p: The Instrument lesson IR.VI.B covers the pilot's side of this approach, and lesson FII.VIII.A sorts approaches into precision, APV and nonprecision; review its first chunk if the groups are new. This lesson adds how you teach the precision approach. The PTS calls an approach precision when it goes to a published DA using approved vertical guidance, and the applicant must fly one to the DA using aircraft navigation equipment for centerline and vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

body.p: **Where the labels differ.** The AIM and IPH say LPV is not a precision approach, even with minima as low as 200 ft HAT [[33:102|AIM 1-1-18b1]] [[29:203|IPH 4-63]], and for alternate planning the IPH treats APVs as nonprecision [[29:146|IPH 4-6]]. The PTS sorts its Tasks by DA versus MDA instead. Teach both, as lesson FII.VIII.A does: AIM words to explain the systems, PTS words to plan the checkride.

**Selection of the appropriate instrument approach chart.** Start with the IPH planning questions: is the weather right for the approach, is the airplane properly equipped, and is the pilot qualified and current [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]? Wind and visibility can leave only one or two usable approaches at an airport [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. Then match the chart to the equipment:

bullets: An ILS needs the localizer: with it out, no ILS approach is authorized; with the glideslope out, the ILS becomes a localizer approach flown on the S-LOC line [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j1]] [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j2]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

"Or" in a title such as ILS or LOC RWY 7 means either system may be used [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]]. An approach keeps its published name when the glideslope is out, and ATC must say the glideslope is unusable when clearing you, except when the title already allows for it, as "ILS or LOC" does [[33:420|AIM 5-4-6d]] [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7h]].
LPV needs WAAS equipment with an AFM statement that it supports LPV; LNAV/VNAV needs approach-approved baro-VNAV or suitable WAAS [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]] [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(c)]].
Some RNAV (GPS) charts also carry an ILS line: the final is the ILS, while the rest of the procedure and the missed approach use GPS criteria [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m3(a)]].

GLS is on its own chart and needs specific aircraft eligibility [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m3(b)]] [[33:107|AIM 1-1-19b]]. Category II and III need special certification of operator, pilot, aircraft and ground equipment; Category I needs only an instrument rating, currency and proper equipment [[29:203|IPH 4-63]].

callout.text: Application: hand the learner the Troy ILS or LOC RWY 7, the Gulfport RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 and the airplane's equipment list, and ask which lines each chart allows and why. Then "NOTAM" the glideslope out and ask again. Choosing is its own element (K1a), and a wrong choice spoils every step after it.

check.q: Your learner's airplane has a WAAS GPS approved for LPV, but its glideslope receiver is placarded inoperative. ATIS says ILS RWY 14 in use; an RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 with LPV is also published. Which approach gives a precision approach for this Task?
check.a: The RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 to the LPV DA: it goes to a DA with approved vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]] and needs WAAS approved for LPV, not a glideslope receiver [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]]. Without the glideslope the ILS would only be a localizer approach to an MDA [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j2]]. Tell ATC at once that a different approach is wanted [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7g]].

chunks.title: The ILS: parts, numbers and why they matter

body.p: Teach the ILS as three jobs: guidance from the localizer and glideslope, range from marker beacons and DME, and visual information from the approach, touchdown zone, centerline and runway lights [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9a3]]. The basic components are the localizer, glideslope and outer marker, plus an inner marker for Category II and III [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(k)]].

head: Part
What it does
Numbers to know
rows: Localizer

body.p: **Why the numbers matter in teaching.** A localizer only 700 ft wide at the threshold is much sharper than a VOR radial, and treating it like one is the first ILS error the IFH lists [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]. The glidepath is about 1,500 ft thick 10 NM out but only a few feet thick at touchdown [[23:280|IFH 9-37]], so a correction that was right at the OM is far too big near the DA.

callout.text: Application: the AIH uses ILS design as its example of integrated training: teach the system on the ground, practice the procedure in a simulator, then verify it in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. A learner who can sketch both beams and say what each needle shows needs much less talking in the airplane.

check.q: Your learner asks why the localizer needle "gets touchier" on short final. What do you say?
check.a: The localizer is angular: about 5° wide and 700 ft wide at the threshold, so the same needle deflection means fewer feet off course as you get closer [[23:280|IFH 9-37]] [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9b2]]. Corrections must get smaller as the course narrows [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

chunks.title: Glideslope sensitivity, false glideslopes and signal limits

body.p: **How sensitive the glideslope is.** Full scale is only about 1.4° from full up to full down, so the needle is very sensitive; with the proper rate of descent set at interception, very small corrections keep the airplane on it [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. The IFH figure shows about 50 ft per dot near the outer marker but only about 8 ft per dot near the middle marker [[23:285|IFH Figure 9-39]]. Above the glidepath the needle points down; below it, up [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

**False glideslopes.** IFH Addendum B, False Courses (November 2019), replaces the IFH 9-40 paragraph on false courses. A glideslope facility also produces false courses at higher angles, about 6° to 12°. Some (false nulls) look like a normal 3° glideslope but are steeper or in the wrong place and can lead to a high descent rate if followed; others are signal reversals, where fly down turns into fly up, and depending on the capture logic the airplane may pitch up. In general reversals occur at 9° and false nulls at 12°, and both may occur around 6°. There may be no warning before a false glideslope is crossed (IFH Addendum B). The AIM tells pilots to be alert approaching glidepath interception, because false courses and reverse sensing occur at angles well above the published path [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d4]].

bullets: Fly the charted altitudes and capture the glideslope from below: then the false courses are not met. Intercepting from above raises the risk of a false capture and of an unstabilized approach (IFH Addendum B).
Brief the glideslope intercept altitude so a false glideslope is not followed by mistake, and cross-check the charted glideslope altitude at the FAF [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].
Keep altitude-versus-distance checks going (IFH Addendum B): 300 ft per NM approximates a 3° path [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
With an autopilot, select approach mode once level at the FAF altitude, so the glideslope is captured from below [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

callout.text: How a false glideslope shows up for your learner: the descent rate needed to keep the needle centered is far above the table. At 90 knots the table gives 478 fpm for 3.0°, but 955 fpm for 6.0° and 1,890 fpm for 12.0° [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]], the angles where false nulls, the kind that look like a glideslope, occur (IFH Addendum B). A needle that stays centered only at double the table rate or more is not the glideslope you briefed.

body.p: **Signal limits.** Vehicles and aircraft near the antennas can disturb the signals; with a ceiling of 800 ft or more and visibility of 2 miles or more, ATC does not protect the critical areas unless the crew asks, and they are not protected at uncontrolled airports [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k2(a)]] [[33:85|AIM 1-1-9k5]]. The glidepath may not be suitable below the lowest DH [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d2]], and Category I signals are not flight inspected below a point 100 ft under the DA [[33:85|AIM 1-1-9k NOTE]]. On a back course, disregard glideslope indications unless the chart specifies a glideslope; false signals there can even make the flag disappear [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d1]].

check.q: On the localizer and cleared for the ILS, your learner is 1,500 ft above the glideslope intercept altitude when the glideslope needle centers, and wants to follow it down. What do you teach?
check.a: Capturing from above raises the risk of a false glideslope and an unstabilized approach (IFH Addendum B). Descend to the published altitudes and intercept at the glideslope intercept altitude [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]]; a real 3° path at 90 knots needs about 478 fpm, so a much higher rate is a warning [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart top to bottom: Troy ILS or LOC RWY 7

body.p: **Pertinent information on the selected instrument approach chart.** Brief an ILS in chart order, the same way every time. The IPH's minimum ILS briefing is the approach name, runway, frequencies, final approach course, glideslope intercept altitude, DA or DH and the missed approach [[29:203|IPH 4-63]]. The chart for this lesson is the Troy ILS or LOC RWY 7, Amdt 9, from 2010 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]: teach from it, and fly only current charts.

body.p: Two traps on this chart. The S-ILS and S-LOC lines are different numbers, 600 versus 880, so the briefing must say which line is being flown. And the remote altimeter note changes the ILS line too: DA 701 and 1 mile with the Montgomery setting [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]], a HAT of 309 ft. Troy's published HAT, 208, is close to the normal Category I value of 200 ft; a published HAT of 250 ft or more may come from signal coverage or obstacle penetrations that the chart does not locate [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

**Failure to have essential knowledge of the information on the instrument approach procedure chart.** On an ILS it shows up as the wrong line of minima, a DA not raised for the altimeter source, a descent below the glideslope intercept altitude before intercepting, or a learner who does not know the missed approach at the DA. The usual cause is a briefing that skipped items; the fix is a complete briefing before the IAF, missed approach included, because the missed approach comes when workload is highest [[23:312|IFH 10-21]] [[29:182|IPH 4-42]].

callout.text: ILS briefing order: name and runway, localizer frequency and ID, final course, glideslope intercept altitude, DA and visibility for your line and category, missed approach [[29:203|IPH 4-63]]. Add the notes, the lights and the glideslope altitude at the FAF for the altimeter cross-check [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].

check.q: Your learner briefs "DA 600, ¾ mile" at Troy, but the local altimeter setting is not available tonight. What changes?
check.a: Use the Montgomery setting: DA 701 and visibility 1 mile for every category on the S-ILS line [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. With no authorized altimeter setting at all, the approach would not be authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

chunks.title: Select, tune, identify and check: ILS, markers and WAAS

body.p: **Selection, tuning, identification, and determination of operational status of ground and aircraft navigation equipment.** Put the primary NAVAID in the radio that still works on battery or emergency power, often Nav 1 [[29:175|IPH 4-35]], and positively identify it before using it for course guidance [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]. Then check every other item the chart requires.

head: Item
Select and tune
Identify and confirm status
rows: Localizer and glideslope
Tune the localizer; the glideslope is usually tuned automatically with it [[23:282|IFH 9-39]]. Set the inbound course on the OBS as a reminder, though it does not move the needle [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]

Morse code, I plus three letters, such as I-TOI [[33:79|AIM 1-1-9b4]]; flags show for an unstable signal or receiver failure [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]; no ID or a T-E-S-T code means maintenance: do not use it [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]
Marker beacons
Receiver on LOW sensitivity for the sharpest indication [[33:82|AIM 1-1-9f1]] [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]
Some receivers take power from another radio, often the ADF, and the test only checks the bulbs; the real check is receiving a marker [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]
Compass locator and ADF
Troy: ADF required, LOM BLOOD on 365 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]
The outer locator sends the first two letters of the localizer ID: TO [[33:82|AIM 1-1-9g2]]
DME
I-TOI is LOC/DME on Chan 26 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]; ILS DME may replace the OM when the procedure specifies it [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9e1]]
Check the readout against the profile: LOM at I-TOI 5.5 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]
LPV
Load the whole approach by name from the database, or by the 5-digit WAAS channel [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m2]] [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d6]]
Cross-check the approach ID, W14A at Gulfport [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d6]] [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]]; after activation the annunciation gives the line to fly [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]
GLS
Select the procedure; the chart gives its approach ID (RPI), which works like the ILS identifier [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m3(b)]]
Be in GLS approach mode before the glidepath intercept point [[33:107|AIM 1-1-19f]]

bullets: Some GPS installations stop GPS navigation whenever any ILS frequency is tuned: then tune the ILS only on the intermediate segment, and retune for a GPS-based missed approach [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m3(a)]].
WAAS MAY NOT BE AVBL NOTAMs are predictions: if the receiver shows LPV on the approach, the vertical guidance may be used [[33:103|AIM 1-1-18c5(a)]].
Report a complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]], and change to another source if the needles misbehave [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13c]].

callout.text: Application: make the setup a spoken item: "108.9, I-TOI identified, Nav 1, course 070 set, markers low, ADF on BLOOD, TO identified, DA 600 bugged." Hearing it said aloud shows you a misunderstanding before it shows on the needles, as in the learner-tells step [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner tunes 108.9 at Troy, sees both needles alive with no flags, and skips the identifier. Why insist on it?
check.a: Removing the identifier is how a facility under maintenance warns pilots that it may be unreliable even though signals are received [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. Identify I-TOI before using it for guidance [[29:157|IPH 4-17]].

chunks.title: Talking to ATC and following the clearance

body.p: **Radio communications with ATC and compliance with ATC clearances, instructions, and procedures.** Most ILS approaches begin with vectors, so teach what each phrase allows before the learner hears it.

head: Situation
What the learner does
rows: "Maintain 2,000 until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway 36 approach"

Hold the assigned altitude until established on a published segment; then published altitudes apply [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. An aircraft is not established while below published approach altitudes [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7f NOTE 2]]
On a vector, no approach clearance yet
Do not turn inbound on the final course [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(c)]]; if about to cross final with no warning, query the controller [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(b)]]
Established on the final course
Stay on it unless cleared otherwise; after the FAF continue inbound and land or fly the missed approach [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(d)]] [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(e)]]
Glideslope out of service
The approach keeps its name; ATC must say the glideslope is unusable when clearing you, unless the title already allows for it, as ILS or LOC does [[33:420|AIM 5-4-6d]] [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7h]]
Ceiling 800 ft or more and 2 miles or more
No critical area protection unless requested; expect possible needle movement, and monitor a coupled autopilot closely [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k2(a)]] [[33:85|AIM 1-1-9k5]]
Not in radar contact
Report leaving the outer marker, or the fix used in lieu of it, inbound [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a2(a)]]
Missed approach
Tell ATC with the reason, fly the published or assigned missed approach, then ask for specific action [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7k]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21f]]

body.p: Tracking the glideslope before the glideslope intercept altitude does not by itself keep the airplane at or above the altitudes at earlier fixes; a pilot who chooses to do it stays responsible for them [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]].

**Incorrect communications procedures or noncompliance with ATC clearances.** On an ILS it looks like a descent on a vector before being established, a turn inbound without an approach clearance, a missed approach with no report, or an approach accepted that the airplane cannot fly. When unsure of a clearance the pilot must ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]], and if a different approach is wanted, say so immediately [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7g]].

callout.text: Application: play ATC from the right seat with realistic vectors, including a late turn-on that leaves the learner high and close in. The answer you want is "unable, request vectors for another try," not a dive at the needle (IFH Addendum B).

check.q: Vectored at 3,000 ft and told "maintain 3,000 until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway 7 approach," your learner starts down the moment the localizer needle comes off the side. Right or wrong?
check.a: Wrong. A needle coming alive is not established on the course. Hold 3,000 until established on the localizer, a published segment, and then use the published altitudes [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].

body.p: **Appropriate aircraft configuration, airspeed, and checklist items.** A stabilized approach keeps speed, descent rate, vertical path and configuration constant in the final stages, which simplifies the decision at the DA; it is strongly recommended for propeller airplanes too, and low-altitude configuration changes should be limited to easy ones [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. The IPH example has the airplane fully configured for landing before glideslope intercept [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

Small airplanes often fly an instrument final well above 1.3 VSO, for example 90 knots, with the gear lowered at glideslope intercept and perhaps an intermediate flap setting [[23:86|IFH 4-9]]. Slowed near 1.3 VSO, speed stability is close to neutral, so pitch and power must be coordinated more precisely [[23:86|IFH 4-9]]. Speed is also a minimums item: faster than the category limit means the higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

body.p: **Failure to accomplish checklist items.** On an ILS: marker receiver off or on HIGH, wrong altimeter setting, DA not bugged or bugged for the wrong line, missed approach altitude never set, autopilot not in approach mode, or an LPV flown without checking the annunciation [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]. The PTS accepts reviewing a checklist after the items are done when reading it during the maneuver would be unsafe or impracticable in a single-pilot operation [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]].

callout.text: Application: tie a short flow to the chart: everything set and briefed before the localizer, configured before the glideslope, a three-item check at intercept, and the LOM cross-check. Have the learner say each item aloud so a skipped one is heard [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner intercepts the glideslope at cruise speed, then slows, adds flaps and lowers the gear while descending. What do you teach?
check.a: Slow and configure before the glideslope, with only planned changes such as the gear at intercept [[23:86|IFH 4-9]], so that speed, rate and configuration stay constant down final [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Big speed and configuration changes late in the approach degrade situational awareness and complicate the decision at the DA [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

body.p: **Adjustments applied to the published DH/DA and visibility criteria for the aircraft approach category.** The authorized DA is the highest of the procedure's DA, the DA prescribed for the pilot in command, and the DA for the equipment available and used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]]. Then work through the adjustments.

bullets: **Category.** VREF, or 1.3 VSO at maximum certificated landing weight if no VREF: A below 91 knots, B 91 to below 121, C 121 to below 141, D 141 to below 166 [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. An airplane may never use a slower category, and faster than the category limit means the higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. At Troy the S-ILS line is 600-¾ for every category, but the S-LOC and circling lines are not [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

**Altimeter source.** Remote setting notes change DAs too: Troy goes to DA 701 and adds ¼ mile, and Gulfport adds 67 ft to all DAs [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]] [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]]. When a second source is authorized and the local setting is not available, baro-VNAV is not authorized, but WAAS receivers may still use the LNAV/VNAV line with the other source [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

**Inoperative components.** Published minimums assume all components and visual aids work; higher minimums apply when they do not, and glideslope-out minimums are published as localizer minimums [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. Read the chart notes first, such as Gulfport's "For inoperative MALSR increase LNAV Cat D visibility to RVR 6000" [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]], then the TPP inoperative components table [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]].

**RVR.** 600/24 means 600 ft MSL and RVR 2,400 [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. If RVR is not reported for the runway, convert the minimum with the 91.175(h) table, for example 2,400 to ½ mile [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)(2)]]. Between table values use the next higher RVR, never interpolate: 1,800 becomes ½ mile [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]].
**Adding visibility to an RVR value.** Convert to miles, add, then convert back to the highest RVR for that visibility: 2000 RVR plus ⅛ mile is ⅝ mile, or 3500 RVR [[2:121|Chart Users' Guide p 121]].

**Category II and III.** Lower minimums need special authorization and equipment [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9i1]], and their DH is measured with a radio altimeter [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Category I needs only an instrument rating, currency and proper equipment [[29:203|IPH 4-63]].

body.p: Category I's lowest minimums are DH 200 ft and RVR 2,400, or RVR 1,800 with touchdown zone and centerline lights, or with an autopilot, flight director or HUD [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9i1(a)]]. The IPH figure shows only the lighting case for RVR 1,800 [[29:210|IPH Figure 4-41]]; teach the AIM's fuller list, and always the chart's own line. On a runway without those lights, RVR 1800 needs a chart note authorizing it with a flight director, autopilot or HUD to the DA, and the AIM says single pilots should not fly it using only a flight director unless a coupled autopilot is also used [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(d)]].

callout.text: Treat the IFH's inoperative-component example, ¼ mile more for an ILS with the ALSF-1 out, as an example, not a rule: the IFH itself sends you to the Inoperative Components table in the TPP [[23:313|IFH 10-22]], which is not in these sources. Teach the learner to read the chart notes, the current TPP table and the NOTAMs.
Highest wins: procedure, pilot, equipment [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]]. Then category speed, altimeter source, inoperative parts, RVR or visibility.

check.q: At Troy your Category A learner must use the Montgomery altimeter setting. What are the S-ILS minimums, and who decides whether there is enough visibility to land?
check.a: DA 701 with 1 mile [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. Landing needs flight visibility of at least the published 1 mile [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]], and only the pilot can judge flight visibility, whatever is reported [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

chunks.title: LPV, LNAV/VNAV and GLS: DA approaches without a localizer

body.p: LPV uses WAAS to give angular lateral and vertical guidance with sensitivities nearly the same as an ILS at similar distances, on purpose, so ILS skills transfer; like an ILS it is flown to a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]]. From the cockpit an LPV looks and flies like an ILS, without ILS critical area limits [[29:166|IPH 4-26]]. GLS gives ILS-like guidance from GPS corrected by a station at the airport and is flown with the same technique as an ILS or LPV final [[33:107|AIM 1-1-19c]] [[33:107|AIM 1-1-19f]].

body.p: **Reading Gulfport.** LPV is DA 227 with RVR 2400, HAT 200; LNAV/VNAV is DA 464 with RVR 5000, HAT 437; LNAV is MDA 440, HAT 413 [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]]. The LNAV HAT (413) is lower than the LNAV/VNAV HAT (437): the IPH says that is a clear sign obstacles below the MDA must be seen; a pilot flying the LNAV line may then use the glide path as a VDA down to the LNAV MDA, with every nonprecision rule applied there [[29:163|IPH 4-23]]. The IFH captions this chart "ILS or LOC Rwy 14," but it is titled RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]].

**What changes in the cockpit.** The receiver announces the best level of service once the approach is active and does not upgrade later; if only the vertical flag appears, the pilot may use the LNAV minima if the operating rules allow [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]. Along-track distance on an LPV goes to a point near the threshold, and the missed approach starts at the DA, not when the distance reads zero [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]]. VDPs and final-segment stepdown altitudes do not apply to LPV or LNAV/VNAV DA lines [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(b)]] [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

check.q: Halfway down an LPV, your learner's receiver loses vertical guidance and shows a vertical flag. What now?
check.a: The receiver will not fail down on its own; the pilot may elect the LNAV minima if the operating rules allow changing approach type after starting [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]. That means an MDA, with final-segment stepdown altitudes applying again [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]]. If in doubt, go missed and tell ATC why [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7k]].

body.p: **Maintenance of altitude, airspeed, and track, where applicable.** You must fly to the instrument pilot skill level while instructing [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], and on final the PTS allows no more than ¾-scale deflection of the lateral or vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]. Before final, the Instrument ACS standards in lesson IR.VI.B are altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:22|IR ACS IR.VI.B.S9]].

head: Phase
Technique to teach
rows: Intercept
Avoid large intercept angles, which usually overshoot; turn to the localizer heading at the first needle movement; an ADF on a locator helps orientation [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]
On the localizer
Hold the inbound heading until the CDI moves; make small drift corrections, reduced as the course narrows, so that by the OM corrections are 2° or less [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]

Set the descent rate for the groundspeed at interception; then adjust pitch for the rate of descent and power for airspeed [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]
OM to MM
The heaviest demand: localizer, pitch and power, the altimeter, and getting ready to land or go missed, all at once [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]
Off the path
Low and slow: add power. Low and fast: pitch up. High and fast: reduce power. High and slow: pitch down [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]

body.p: **Wind.** A crosswind shows up as the heading that keeps the localizer centered; find it early with small corrections that shrink as the course narrows [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. A headwind or tailwind changes groundspeed, so the descent rate that holds the glideslope changes too (next chunk). Low-level wind shear, a PTS emphasis item, is the dangerous case: a tailwind shearing to a headwind makes the airplane balloon above the glidepath, a headwind shearing to a tailwind makes it sink below, and a headwind shear followed by a tailwind or downdraft is worst, because power is already back and the nose already low [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]. Teach the learner to watch for it early and go missed at the first sign [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

**Faulty basic instrument flying technique.** The IFH's ILS operational errors: treating the localizer like a VOR radial, disorientation from poor planning and relying on one receiver, a large localizer intercept angle, and chasing the CDI and glidepath needles, especially after too little study of the approach [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]. In the descent itself: chasing the VSI, not trimming and overcontrolling pitch [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The fix is a planned rate, trim, and small corrections.

callout.text: Application: on the first ILS lessons, say the needle positions and trends aloud ("half a dot high, steady") so the learner hears what a small error looks like. Then stop talking and have the learner call them [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Crossing the LOM, your learner is still making 10° heading corrections on the localizer. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
check.a: The drift correction was not found early: by the OM it should be accurate enough that heading corrections are 2° or less [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. Large corrections chase the needle, a listed ILS error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]].

chunks.title: Descent rate for the groundspeed, and what the MFD adds

body.p: **Establishment and maintenance of an appropriate rate of descent during the final approach segment.** The glideslope is fixed to the ground, so the rate that holds it depends on groundspeed. With the proper rate set at glideslope interception, only very small corrections are needed [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

body.p: **Teach it with wind.** A 90-knot approach into a 15-knot headwind has a 75-knot groundspeed and needs about 398 fpm; with a 15-knot tailwind, 105 knots over the ground, it needs about 557 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. A learner who flies a memorized 500 fpm sinks below the glideslope in the headwind and drifts above it in the tailwind. Below 1,000 ft AGL a descent rate above about 1,000 fpm is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Application: work the tailwind case before choosing the runway.

**Uses of the MFD and other parameters to maintain desired flightpath.** An MFD can show a moving map, approach charts, terrain and weather [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. A GPS gives track and groundspeed, and a heading that keeps track and bearing matched holds the course [[23:272|IFH 9-29]]; the actual groundspeed is what goes into the descent table [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. A PFD shows the same glideslope deviation as the round dial [[23:285|IFH Figure 9-39]]; trend vectors help, but pilots new to them tend to fixate, so use them with the primary instruments [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. A flight director gives steering commands and does not mean the autopilot is flying [[23:119|IFH 5-24]], and a coupled approach still needs close monitoring and readiness to take over [[33:85|AIM 1-1-9k5]]. Treat the displays as a supplement, not a replacement for the charts, and keep track of position on the chart in case a screen fails [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

callout.text: Application: the PTS expects you to show automation management with the autopilot and displays installed [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]]. Fly one ILS by hand using the MFD groundspeed and the table, and one coupled while the learner monitors and calls deviations, then compare the workload.

check.q: Crossing BLOOD at Troy with the glideslope centered, your learner's altimeter reads 2,100 while the chart shows 1936. What do you do?
check.a: Treat it as a failed cross-check: the charted glideslope altitude at the FAF is there so pilots can cross-check their altimeters and verify the indications [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]. Check the altimeter setting and the identifier; if the indications still disagree, change to another source or go missed and ask ATC for a new clearance [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13c]].

chunks.title: At the DA: land straight in, circle, or go missed

body.p: **Factors that should be considered in determining whether: (1) the approach should be continued straight-in to a landing; (2) a circling approach to a landing should be made; or (3) a missed approach should be performed.** On a precision approach the MAP is the point where the airplane reaches the DA on the glidepath [[29:181|IPH 4-41]], so the decision is made there, without delay [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.175(c): continue below the DA only when the airplane is continuously in position to descend to the intended runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers, the flight visibility is at least the published visibility, and at least one listed visual reference is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. With the approach lights alone, not below 100 ft above TDZE unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. Not met at the DA, or at any time after it until touchdown: missed approach immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

head: Decision
Factors from the sources
rows: (1) Straight-in landing

91.175(c) met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; flight visibility at least the published value to land, whatever is reported [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]; still stabilized, with no descent rate above about 1,000 fpm [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]
(2) Circle to land

Needed to land on another runway, or when no straight-in minimums exist [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. Plan it early: descend only to the circling MDA, not the DA, and stay at or above it until in position for a normal descent to the runway [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]; the circling MAP is the nonprecision one, by timing or a fix, not the DA [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]. Circling from an ILS needs a localizer line of minima, and is prohibited from a GLS or from an RNAV (GPS) without an LNAV line [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]. Troy circling is 940-1 for A and B, an MDA [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]] [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]
(3) Missed approach

No required reference or visibility at the DA [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]; references lost after it; the approach becomes unstabilized or the runway is blocked [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]; ATC directs it [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; signs of wind shear [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]

body.p: **What the approach lights allow.** In Figure 9-36 red lights appear only in the ALSF-2 and ALSF-1 patterns, not in SSALR/MALSR, MALSF or ODALS [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]]. So a learner who sees only a MALSR at the DA may continue if the visibility is there, but not below 100 ft above TDZE until another listed reference, such as the threshold or runway lights, is distinctly visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. The Troy chart shows no approach lighting box [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]], only MIRL on Runway 7-25 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]], so at the DA the learner must see a listed reference on the runway itself, such as the threshold, the runway or its lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

**After the decision.** Approaches with vertical guidance make the transition to visual safer, because the airplane is already stabilized when the references appear [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Flying into fog can create an illusion of pitching up, and pilots who do not recognize it often steepen the approach abruptly [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]]. A missed approach starts with climb attitude and climb power, configuring for climb, the published turn and a call to ATC [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; Task C, lesson FII.VIII.C, covers it in full.

check.q: At Troy's DA of 600 your learner sees the runway lights clearly, and the flight visibility looks like a mile. The last report was ½ mile. May the learner continue and land?
check.a: Yes, if 91.175(c) is met: runway lights are a listed reference [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]], and landing depends on flight visibility of at least the published ¾ mile [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. Only the pilot can determine flight visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

body.p: **Inappropriate application of DH/DA.** This is the precision approach's own common error. A DA is not an MDA. An MDA is the lowest altitude to which descent is authorized until the 91.175 conditions are met [[29:159|IPH 4-19]] [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]]; a DA is where the missed approach is started if the visual references for landing are not established [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]].

body.p: **What a DA does allow.** Obstacle clearance is provided for a momentary descent below the DA while transitioning from the final approach to the missed approach, and the airplane should continue along the final course to the threshold waypoint or MAP before turning [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]. A small sink during a prompt go-around is designed for; a deliberate descent below the DA to look for the runway is not.

callout.text: Landing expectancy and pride are the usual reasons a go-around starts late [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. In training, never let a learner go below the DA without references "to see what happens"; guard the controls and take them early, since a learner should never exceed the instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: At the DA your learner calls "minimums, nothing yet" and holds the altitude for a few seconds while looking. What do you say?
check.a: That treats the DA like an MDA. With no required reference at the DA the missed approach must start immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]], and any delay adds risk from obstacles in the visual segment [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Go missed now, and in the debrief tie the callout to an immediate decision.

chunks.title: Brief, demonstrate and talk it through

body.p: **Demonstrates and simultaneously explains a precision instrument approach from an instructional standpoint.** The explanation must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting, while you fly to the instrument pilot skill level [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Introduction]]. The precision approach goes to the DA in simulated or actual instrument conditions, and the evaluator may ask for a landing or a missed approach at the end [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]]. The Area NOTE has the evaluator select Tasks A and B with C, D or E; its no-gyro requirement applies to a nonprecision approach, covered in FII.VIII.A [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]].

Use the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], with the telling-and-doing steps in the airplane [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Before flight, brief the exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] and when and how the view-limiting device goes on and off [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]]. A safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with appropriate category and class ratings and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].
**A talk-through you can use at Troy** (put in your POH speeds and power settings):

bullets: "Cleared ILS 7, maintain 2,500 until established. 108.9, I-TOI identified, course 070 set, markers low, ADF on BLOOD [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]] [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]."

"Localizer alive: turning to 070 now, small corrections from here [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]. Established inside MAKEY, so the published altitude applies: down to 2,000, the glideslope intercept altitude, to capture from below [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]."

"At approach speed and configured before the glideslope [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]. Glideslope centered: power back, nose down. Groundspeed 75, so about 400 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. Missed approach altitude set [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]."
"BLOOD: chart says 1936, altimeter agrees, glideslope centered [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]. The needles get sharper now, so smaller corrections [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]."

"Approaching minimums, still on the needles, looking for the runway. Minimums, 600: runway lights in sight and the visibility is there, continuing to land; or nothing in sight, go around now [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]."

callout.text: Positive exchange of flight controls: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls." Add a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: During your demonstration you drift a dot high while explaining the wind. What should you do?
check.a: Correct it and say so at once: when a demonstration does not match the explanation, the deviation should be acknowledged and explained immediately [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Stay within ¾-scale deflection [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

body.p: **Analyzes and corrects simulated common errors.** On the checkride the evaluator acts as a learner and flies the errors on purpose. Name the error, say what you see, give the cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it. The listed errors may not appear in the references, the evaluator will not simulate anything unsafe [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]], and a realistic distraction is part of every test [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]].

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how you teach it
rows: Chart knowledge (K2a)
Wrong line of minima, DA not raised for the altimeter source, no missed approach plan
Briefing skipped or partial
Brief in chart order, missed approach included [[29:203|IPH 4-63]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]
Communications and clearances (K2b)
Descent on a vector before established; turn inbound without a clearance; no missed approach report
Not knowing when published altitudes apply; reluctance to ask
Last assigned altitude until established [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]; ask when unsure [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
Checklist items (K2c)
Markers off, missed approach altitude not set, wrong altimeter setting, LPV annunciation unchecked
Workload, no flow
Set up and brief before the localizer [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]; check the annunciation [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]
Basic instrument technique (K2d)
Localizer flown like a VOR, big intercept overshoot, chasing the needles or the VSI
No planned rate, large corrections, no trim [[23:285|IFH 9-42]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Rate for the groundspeed at intercept, trim, small corrections [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]
DH/DA (K2e)
Leveling at the DA, descending below it to look, wrong DA
Landing expectancy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; MDA habits
Decide at the DA; missed approach when 91.175(c) is not met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct: when the learner thinks aloud you can tell a misconception from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let a learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but on an ILS that never means sinking below the glideslope near the ground: the AIM says to avoid flying below the glide path to keep obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]]. To test real understanding, change something, such as the wind, the runway or an LPV instead of the ILS; a learner who only memorized will struggle [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: The evaluator, as your learner, flies the ILS a full dot low from the LOM inward in a headwind and says "close enough." Name the error, the cause and the fix.
check.a: Faulty basic instrument flying technique (K2d): the descent rate was not reset for the lower groundspeed, so the airplane sinks below the path, where obstacle clearance is not assured [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]]. Fix: low and slow needs power, low and fast needs pitch up [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]; then set the table rate for the groundspeed [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

scenario.title: A headwind ILS into Troy on a remote altimeter
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument learner, about 30 hours into training, flies a fixed-gear Category A trainer with round dials, one nav radio with a glideslope, a marker receiver, an ADF and an IFR GPS. Tonight's lesson is the ILS or LOC RWY 7 at Troy (Figure 10-11), flown at 90 knots on final under a view-limiting device, ending in a full-stop landing if the approach works out. The local altimeter setting is not available, and the wind is 070 at 15. The weather is VMC with a high ceiling, and you are both instructor and safety pilot.

questions.q: What do you brief on the ground about the flight controls, the device and your role?
questions.a: The three-step exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], when and how the device goes on and off [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]], and that you keep the lookout as safety pilot [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. Agree that you will take the controls early if the airplane gets low on the glideslope near the ground, since a learner should never exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: Which minimums apply, and how do you make sure the learner uses them?
questions.a: With the Montgomery setting: DA 701 and 1 mile on the S-ILS line for Category A [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]], a HAT of 309 ft. The authorized DA is the highest that applies [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]], so have the learner brief it aloud and bug 701, not the 600 printed on the line.

questions.q: Approach says, "Five miles from BLOOD, turn right heading 040, maintain 2,500 until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway 7 approach." The learner wants to descend now. What do you teach?
questions.a: Hold 2,500 until established on the localizer; then the published altitude for that segment applies, here 2,000 between MAKEY and BLOOD, the glideslope intercept altitude [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. On the localizer outside MAKEY the charted altitude is 2,600, and an aircraft below a published approach altitude is not established [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7f NOTE 2]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]; that is why the vector here ends inside MAKEY. Capture the glideslope from below at 2,000, not from above, to avoid a false glideslope and an unstabilized approach (IFH Addendum B).

questions.q: With the wind 070 at 15, what descent rate should the learner set, and what happens with the usual 500 fpm?
questions.a: Groundspeed is about 75 knots, so about 398 fpm for 3.0° [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. At 500 fpm the airplane sinks below the glideslope, and below the glide path obstacle clearance is not assured [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]].

questions.q: At 701 you leave the device on to simulate no runway. The learner says, "The chart says 600, I'll go down to 600 and look." What do you say and do?
questions.a: Go around now: tonight's authorized DA is 701 [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]], and with no required reference at the DA the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. Name the error, inappropriate application of DA, and fly the missed approach as published: climb to 1300, then a climbing right turn to 2200 direct BLOOD [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

questions.q: How do you run the debrief?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then your detailed assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Base it on standards suited to the learner's stage and look at each element, such as the briefing, the descent rate and the DA, not just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: Demonstrate an ILS, or an LPV, to the DA while explaining the briefing, setup and identification, the glideslope capture from below, the descent rate for the groundspeed, the FAF altitude cross-check and the decision at the DA, holding instrument pilot standards [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] and no more than ¾-scale deflection [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].
skills.practice: Fly the Troy talk-through aloud in a simulator first, then in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], in the same order every time you brief it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Change the wind each time so the descent rate changes [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

skills.do: As the evaluator flies the K2 errors (chart knowledge, radio and clearance mistakes, missed checklist items, faulty technique, misuse of the DA), name each one, say what the instruments show, explain the cause and give the fix and the way you would teach it.
skills.practice: Trade seats with another applicant and fly the errors in the table on purpose; correct them by thinking aloud, so you can tell a misconception from a motor-skill error [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks whether an LPV flown to its DA counts as the precision approach on the checkride, since the AIM calls LPV an APV. What is the best answer?
options: No: only an ILS, GLS or PAR counts as a precision approach for the test
Yes: the PTS counts a standard approach to a DA with approved vertical guidance
Only if the LPV line goes as low as 200 ft HAT with ½ mile visibility
Only when the receiver also annunciates that LNAV/VNAV is available
quiz.why: The PTS defines a precision approach as a standard approach to a published DA using approved vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]. The AIM does call LPV an APV [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]] [[33:102|AIM 1-1-18b1]], which makes the second option tempting, but that is the AIM's grouping, not the PTS test.

quiz.q: Which ILS component, if it fails, means no ILS approach is authorized at all?
options: The localizer
The glideslope
The middle marker
The approach lights
quiz.why: When the localizer fails, an ILS approach is not authorized; when the glideslope fails, the ILS reverts to a localizer approach [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j1]] [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j2]]. A middle marker is no longer required [[33:82|AIM 1-1-9f2(b)]], and inoperative lights raise the minimums [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

quiz.q: Cleared for the ILS but well above the glideslope intercept altitude, your learner finds the glideslope needle centered, and keeping it there at 90 knots takes about 1,900 fpm. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A strong tailwind on the final approach
An altimeter set for the wrong airport
Normal for a 3° glideslope at 90 knots
A false glideslope at a steeper angle
quiz.why: The table gives 478 fpm for 3.0° but 1,890 fpm for 12.0° at 90 knots [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. False nulls, which look like a normal glideslope, occur in general near 12° and lead to a high descent rate if followed (IFH Addendum B) [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d4]]. A tailwind raises the rate, but nowhere near four times.

quiz.q: At Troy, without the local altimeter setting, what are the S-ILS 7 minimums for Category A?
options: DA 600 and ¾ mile
DA 720 and 1 mile
DA 701 and 1 mile
DA 701, still ¾ mile
quiz.why: Use the Montgomery setting: increase all DA to 701 and S-ILS 7 visibility for all categories by ¼ mile, so ¾ becomes 1 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. 720 would be 600 plus the 120 ft MDA increase, which applies only to MDAs.

quiz.q: Vectored at 3,000 ft, your learner hears "maintain 3,000 until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway 7 approach." When may the learner descend?
options: Once established on the localizer, then published altitudes
Right away, since the approach clearance includes the descent
Only after crossing the LOM inbound on the glideslope
As soon as the glideslope needle starts to come down
quiz.why: Keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment; then the published altitudes apply [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. Waiting for the LOM asks more than the rule does, and diving at the needle from above invites a false glideslope (IFH Addendum B).

quiz.q: Your learner flies 500 fpm on every ILS. Today the groundspeed on final is 105 knots. What rate does the table give for a 3.0° glideslope?
options: 398 fpm
478 fpm
557 fpm
637 fpm
quiz.why: Read the 3.0° row in the 105-knot column: 557 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. At 500 fpm the airplane would drift above the glideslope; 478 is the 90-knot value and 637 the 120-knot value.

quiz.q: At the DA your learner sees only a MALSR, and the flight visibility is at the published value. How far may the learner descend using the approach lights alone?
options: To touchdown, since the lights lead right to the runway
To 100 ft above TDZE, then another reference is needed
Not below the DA; approach lights are not a listed reference
To 200 ft above TDZE; then red bars must be in sight
quiz.why: Using the approach lights, no descent below 100 ft above TDZE unless the red terminating or red side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], and the MALSR drawing has no red lights [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]]. The approach light system is the first listed reference, so the third option is wrong.

quiz.q: On an LPV your learner reaches the DA with no runway in sight, but the along-track distance still reads 0.6 NM. What do you teach?
options: Fly on to 0.0 NM, the real MAP
Level off until the distance reads zero
Descend 50 ft, then go missed if needed
Go missed at the DA now
quiz.why: On LPV and LNAV/VNAV the missed approach is based on reaching the DA without the required references and must not wait for the distance to reach zero [[33:106|AIM 1-1-18d7]]. On a precision or APV approach the MAP is at the DA on the glidepath [[29:190|IPH 4-50]].

quiz.q: Which practice best protects your learner from capturing a false glideslope?
options: Fly the charted altitudes and capture from below
Set the marker receiver to high sensitivity
Intercept from above to stay clear of terrain
Arm approach mode early while still high above
quiz.why: Captured from below at the charted altitudes, the false courses are not met; intercepting from above raises the risk (IFH Addendum B). The IPH suggests selecting approach mode once level at the FAF altitude for the same reason [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

quiz.q: Because of gusts, your Category A learner will fly the final at 125 knots. Which statement is right?
options: Stay with Category A, the certified category
Use Category B minimums, the next category up
Use Category C minimums for the speed flown
Category only matters for circling minimums
quiz.why: 125 knots is in Category C, 121 to below 141 [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], and a faster approach must use the higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Straight-in lines can differ by category too, such as Troy's S-LOC line [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

quiz.q: The ceiling is 1,000 ft and the visibility 3 miles. ATC says nothing about the ILS critical areas. What should your learner expect?
options: Full protection, since the airport has a tower
Protection only for a coupled autopilot approach
No effect, because ground monitors catch it
No protection; traffic may move the needles
quiz.why: With a ceiling of 800 ft or more and visibility of 2 miles or more, ATC provides no critical area protection unless the crew asks [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k2(a)]], and ground monitors can miss interference [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13a]].

quiz.q: Near the middle marker one dot of glideslope deflection is only about 8 ft, against about 50 ft at the outer marker. What should your learner do with that fact?
options: Ignore the glideslope once inside the middle marker
Make smaller corrections as the runway gets closer
Use bigger pitch changes to keep up near the runway
Switch to the VSI and stop watching the needle
quiz.why: The figure shows about 50 ft per dot at the OM and 8 ft at the MM [[23:285|IFH Figure 9-39]]; with the right rate set, very small corrections keep the airplane on the glideslope [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. Chasing the needles is a listed error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]].

quiz.q: Your learner loads an RNAV (GPS) approach with LPV, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV lines, and the receiver annunciates "LNAV available" before the FAF. What can be flown?
options: LNAV, to its MDA
LPV, since the chart has it
LNAV/VNAV, the next line down
Only the circling line
quiz.why: If the signal does not support vertical guidance, the receiver reads LNAV available, and that is the level of service for the approach [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]. LNAV is published as an MDA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(e)]].

final_quiz.q: At Gulfport the LNAV MDA of 440 has a HAT of 413, lower than the LNAV/VNAV DA of 464 with a HAT of 437. What does that tell your learner?
options: LNAV is the more precise of the two lines
LNAV/VNAV is not authorized at Gulfport
Obstacles below the MDA must be seen and avoided
The LNAV/VNAV DA is a charting error
final_quiz.why: When LNAV has a lower HAT than a line with a glide path, it is a clear sign that obstacles exist below the MDA and must be seen; on the LNAV line the glide path may be used as a VDA down to the MDA, with every nonprecision rule applied there [[29:163|IPH 4-23]] [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]].

final_quiz.q: A localizer course is normally about 5° wide. How far off the centerline, in degrees, is a full-scale deflection?
options: About 1.25°
About 5°
About 10°
About 2.5°
final_quiz.why: With a 5° course, full scale shows when the aircraft is 2.5° either side of the centerline [[23:280|IFH 9-37]]. That sensitivity is why tracking it like a VOR radial is a listed error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner levels off at the DA "just for a few seconds" to look for the runway. Which common error from this Task is it?
options: Faulty basic instrument technique
Inappropriate application of DH/DA
Failure to accomplish checklist items
Noncompliance with ATC clearances
final_quiz.why: A DA is where the missed approach must start without the required references [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]], and any delay there adds risk from obstacles in the visual segment [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. The altitude may be held perfectly, so it is not a flying-technique error.

final_quiz.q: Your learner thinks the TCH is where the glideslope needle centers over the threshold. What is it really?
options: The planned height of the glideslope antenna over it
The wheel height over the threshold in a normal landing
The height of the DA above the touchdown zone elevation
The lowest height where the glideslope can be used
final_quiz.why: The TCH is a planning reference for where the glideslope antenna should be if the airplane stays on the glidepath, not the actual on-course height [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d6]]. The wheels cross lower, and about 20 to 30 ft is a comfortable wheel height [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d7]]; the DA's height above TDZE is the HAT [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner sets the radio altimeter bug to 200 ft for a Category I ILS and plans to use it as the minimum. What do you teach?
options: Fine: the Category I DH is 200 ft on the radio altimeter
Set both bugs and go missed at whichever comes first
Use 200 ft above the airport elevation instead
Use the barometric DA; radio DHs are for Category II and III
final_quiz.why: A DA is expressed in feet MSL [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]], and Category II and III DHs are measured with a radio altimeter [[29:160|IPH 4-20]] [[34:334|AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary]]. Bug the chart's DA on the altimeter and brief it [[29:175|IPH 4-35]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner continues below the DA with the runway lights in sight. When is a missed approach still required?
options: Never; once below the DA the learner is committed to land
Only if the tower calls for a go-around
If the required reference or visibility is lost
Only once below 100 ft above touchdown zone
final_quiz.why: The missed approach is required whenever the 91.175(c) conditions are not met at the DA and at any time after that until touchdown [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]; the IPH adds a rejected landing for an obstruction on the runway or an unstabilized approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

final_quiz.q: After the Troy ILS to Runway 7, your Category A learner must circle to land on Runway 25. Which statement is right?
options: Circling from an ILS is never allowed
Circle at or above 940, the circling MDA
Circle at 600, the S-ILS DA, until aligned
Circle at 880, the S-LOC 7 MDA
final_quiz.why: Circling from an ILS is allowed when the chart has a localizer line of minima [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]. Troy's Category A circling minimum is 940-1 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]], an MDA [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

final_quiz.q: On a published segment with fixes before the FAF, your learner tracks the glideslope before reaching the glideslope intercept altitude. Who is responsible for the altitudes at those fixes?
options: The pilot, who must still meet each fix altitude
ATC, since the vectors already clear the terrain
No one: the glideslope guarantees the clearance
The autopilot, once it is coupled to the ILS
final_quiz.why: Tracking the glideslope before the intercept altitude does not necessarily ensure compliance with altitudes at preceding fixes; the pilot remains responsible for them [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]].

final_quiz.q: Near a storm on the ILS, your learner's airspeed jumps and the airplane balloons above the glideslope, so the learner pulls power and lowers the nose. Why is this the dangerous case?
options: The glideslope signal reverses above the glidepath
Ballooning means a false glideslope was captured
An airspeed jump means the pitot tube is icing
A tailwind may follow with power low and nose low
final_quiz.why: A headwind shear followed by a tailwind or downdraft shear is particularly dangerous because the pilot has just reduced power and lowered the nose; be ready to go missed at the first sign of wind shear [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

final_quiz.q: The chart minimum is RVR 1800, but RVR is not reported for the runway. What visibility does your learner need?
options: ⅜ mile, by interpolating
¼ mile, the next lower row
½ mile, using the 2400 row
1 mile, to be on the safe side
final_quiz.why: Convert with the RVR table; for a value between entries use the next higher RVR and do not interpolate, so 1800 becomes ½ mile [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner bugs DA 600 at Troy although the briefing included the Montgomery altimeter setting. Which rule makes 701 the DA?
options: 91.175(h): converting RVR to visibility
91.175(b): the highest applicable DA
91.175(i): keep the last assigned altitude
91.175(k): the ILS components
final_quiz.why: The authorized DA is the highest of the procedure's, the pilot's and the equipment's [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]], and the procedure itself raises all DAs to 701 with the Montgomery setting [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

final_quiz.q: Which telling-and-doing step lets you catch a learner's misunderstanding of the ILS before the learner is busy flying it?
options: Learner tells, instructor does
Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
The evaluation after the flight
final_quiz.why: In the learner-tells, instructor-does step a misunderstanding can be corrected before the learner becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: Using the IPH rule of thumb, what descent rate holds a 3° path at 110 knots groundspeed?
options: 330 fpm
440 fpm
660 fpm
550 fpm
final_quiz.why: Multiply groundspeed by 5 for a 3° path: 110 × 5 = 550 fpm [[29:116|IPH 3-4]]. The table's 3.0° row runs from 478 fpm at 90 knots to 637 at 120, which brackets it [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

final_quiz.q: Why does an LPV approach have no ILS-style critical area limits?
options: ATC always protects them for WAAS
LPV minimums are too high to matter
No ground transmitters at the runway
The receiver filters signals below 200 ft
final_quiz.why: LPV procedures need no ground-based transmitters at the airport, which removes the critical area limitations of an ILS [[29:165|IPH 4-25]] [[29:166|IPH 4-26]].

final_quiz.q: Before the checkride flight, which item does the PTS say you and the evaluator should agree on and brief?
options: The evaluator's planned system failures, in exact order
When and how the view-limiting device goes on and off
The total instrument time logged in your logbook
That no distractions will be used during the test flight
final_quiz.why: The PTS asks applicant and evaluator to set and brief before flight when and how the view-limiting device is put on and removed [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]], and it requires a realistic distraction during the flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]]. The preflight briefing should also include the exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: Not in radar contact on the ILS, which report does your learner owe ATC without being asked?
options: Reaching the glideslope intercept altitude
Passing 1,000 ft above the airport
First sighting of the approach lights
Leaving the outer marker or its substitute inbound
final_quiz.why: When not in radar contact, report leaving the outer marker, or the fix used in lieu of it, inbound on final for a precision approach [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a2(a)]]. A missed approach is always reported [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(d)]].

takeaways: For the checkride, a precision approach is a standard approach to a published DA with approved vertical guidance: ILS, GLS, LPV or LNAV/VNAV.
Brief the chart in order and say which line you fly; S-ILS and S-LOC are different numbers.
The authorized DA is the highest of procedure, pilot and equipment; then adjust for category, altimeter source, inoperative parts and RVR.
Capture the glideslope from below at the charted altitude; a centered needle that needs a very high descent rate warns of a false glideslope.
Set the descent rate for the groundspeed at intercept, then make small corrections that shrink as the runway nears.
Cross-check the altimeter with the glideslope altitude at the FAF.
A DA is a decision point, not a floor: without the 91.175(c) conditions, go missed at once; only a brief sink during a prompt go-around is protected.
Demonstrate and explain in the same order, then name each error, its cause and its fix.
cfi_notes: Classification: the AIM and IPH call LPV and LNAV/VNAV APVs and say LPV is not a precision approach [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]] [[29:203|IPH 4-63]], and the IPH counts APVs as nonprecision for alternate planning [[29:146|IPH 4-6]]. The PTS puts every approach to a DA with approved vertical guidance in this Task. Teach both, as lesson FII.VIII.A does.

False glideslopes: IFH 9-40 puts the lowest false course at about 9° to 12° [[23:283|IFH 9-40]], but IFH Addendum B (November 2019) replaces that paragraph: about 6° to 12°, reversals near 9°, false nulls near 12°, both possible near 6°, and possibly no warning. Teach the addendum; lesson IR.VI.B now does too.

Glideslope antenna offset and angle differ by source: the AIM says 250 to 650 ft from the centerline and normally 3° [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d2]] [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d3]]; the IFH text says 400 to 600 ft and 2.5° to 3.5°, up to 4° [[23:280|IFH 9-37]]; IFH Figure 9-33 says 250 to 600 ft [[23:279|IFH Figure 9-33]]. Don't teach any one of these as exact.

Category I RVR 1,800: the AIM allows it with touchdown zone and centerline lights, or with an autopilot, flight director or HUD [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9i1(a)]]; IPH Figure 4-41 shows only the lighting case [[29:210|IPH Figure 4-41]]. Without those lights the chart must carry a note authorizing RVR 1800 with FD, AP or HUD, and the AIM advises single pilots not to use a flight director alone for it [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(d)]]. Teach the AIM, then the chart's own line.

DH versus DA: IFH 1-23 says precision approaches use a DH referenced to HAT [[23:42|IFH 1-23]], but 14 CFR 1.1 defines DA in feet MSL and DH in feet above ground [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]], and charts publish DA in feet MSL with the HAT beside it [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. Teach the regulation and the chart.

Captions: IFH Figure 10-9 is captioned "ILS or LOC Rwy 14" but shows the Gulfport RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]]; Figure 10-11 is captioned "ILS RWY 7" but the chart is ILS or LOC RWY 7 [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. Both charts date from 2010; brief and fly only current charts.

Configuration: IFH 4-9 has a small airplane lowering the gear at glideslope intercept [[23:86|IFH 4-9]], while the IPH example is fully configured before intercept [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]. Both aim at a stable final; use the POH and keep late changes small [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

How it is tested: the evaluator selects Tasks A and B with C, D or E [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]]; the precision approach goes to the DA using aircraft equipment for centerline and vertical guidance in simulated or actual IMC, ending in a landing or missed approach at the evaluator's discretion [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]]. With an installed IFR RNAV system you must also show approach proficiency with it [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]], and one precision approach not flown in the airplane may be done in a qualified FSTD [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:49|PTS Appendix 1]].

Examiners like to ask: why a HAT is sometimes above 200 ft, what the glideslope altitude at the FAF is for, how to recognize a false glideslope, what changes when the glideslope fails, how LPV differs from an ILS, what a momentary descent below the DA means, and the 100 ft approach light rule.
gaps: No source here gives the current TPP Inoperative Components table or the current rate of descent table; only older IFH samples are available.
IFH Addendum B is named in text only; it is not one of the citable resources in this build.

The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances except the ¾-scale deflection [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]; the ±100 ft, ±10° and ±10 knot figures are the Instrument ACS standards [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:22|IR ACS IR.VI.B.S9]], also taught in lesson IR.VI.B.
No source here says how a particular autopilot or GPS captures or rejects a false glideslope; Addendum B points to the aircraft's operating and training manuals.
Approach speeds, power settings, flap settings and when to lower the gear for a given trainer come from its POH/AFM, which is not in the sources.

Blue light, two dashes per second
Amber light, about 200 ft on the glide path
White light, Category II decision point

activities.title: True or false: glideslope traps and signal limits
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Capturing the glideslope from below at the charted altitudes keeps your learner away from false glideslopes.
cards.why: True. Flown at the charted altitudes with the glideslope captured from below, the false courses are not met (IFH Addendum B); they lie well above the published path [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d4]].

cards.s: A false glideslope always gives a flag or other warning before the airplane crosses it.
cards.why: False. There may be no warning before crossing a false glideslope (IFH Addendum B); getting established on one causes confusion or a very high descent rate [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

cards.s: On a Category I ILS the glideslope is good guidance all the way to the runway, with or without references.
cards.why: False. The glidepath may not be suitable below the lowest DH [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d2]], and signals more than 100 ft below the DA are not flight inspected [[33:85|AIM 1-1-9k NOTE]].

cards.s: With a 900 ft ceiling and 3 miles, ATC protects the ILS critical areas whether or not you ask.
cards.why: False. At 800 ft and 2 miles or better, no critical area protection is provided unless the crew requests it [[33:84|AIM 1-1-9k2(a)]].

cards.s: The published TCH is the height of the actual on-course glideslope indication over the threshold.
cards.why: False. It is a planning height for the glideslope antenna, not the actual on-course height [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d6]].

cards.s: On a localizer back course, disregard glideslope indications unless the chart specifies a glideslope.
cards.why: True. False glideslope signals in the back course area can even make the flag disappear [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d1]].

activities.title: Descent rates and minimums
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Troy ILS, 90 knots indicated with a 15-knot headwind, so 75 knots groundspeed. What rate does the table give for 3.0°?
Same approach with a 15-knot tailwind, 105 knots groundspeed. What rate does the table give for 3.0°?
Using the IPH rule of thumb, what descent rate holds a 3° path at 120 knots groundspeed?
items.why: Groundspeed × 5: 120 × 5 = 600 fpm [[29:116|IPH 3-4]]; the table gives 637 [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

items.q: Troy with the Montgomery altimeter setting: DA 701 and TDZE 392. What is the HAT?
items.why: 701 - 392 = 309 ft; HAT is the DA's height above TDZE [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

items.q: Using 300 ft per NM, about how high above TDZE should the airplane be 3 NM from the threshold on a 3° path?
A learner follows a 12.0° false glideslope at 90 knots groundspeed. What descent rate does the table show?
items.why: 12.0° row, 90-knot column: 1,890 fpm, about four times the 478 fpm of a 3.0° path [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]; false nulls, which look like a normal glideslope, occur in general near 12° (IFH Addendum B).

activities.title: Checkride: the examiner flies the ILS errors
activities.intro: You are the CFII applicant. The examiner, playing your learner, flies the Troy ILS or LOC RWY 7 with the Montgomery altimeter setting in a 15-knot headwind and makes errors on purpose. Choose what you say each time.

steps.s: On a vector at 2,500 ft, right after "maintain 2,500 until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway 7," the examiner starts down.
options: Let it go; the clearance includes descent
Name it: hold 2,500 until established on the localizer
Have the examiner climb to the 3,500 MSA
Ask Approach to approve the descent
steps.why: On a vector, keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].

steps.s: Established, the examiner lets the glideslope needle peg full fly-down, then pushes over to 1,200 fpm to catch it.
options: Good: catching the glideslope fast is the goal
Fine, as long as the needle centers by BLOOD
Name it: intercept from below at 2,000 with about 400 fpm
Ignore the glideslope and fly the LOC line
steps.why: Intercepting from above raises the risk of a false glideslope and an unstabilized approach (IFH Addendum B); with a 75-knot groundspeed the table gives about 398 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]], and over about 1,000 fpm low is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

steps.s: On the glideslope the examiner holds 500 fpm and slowly sinks a dot below the path.
options: Name it: 75 knots over the ground needs about 400 fpm
Fine: 500 fpm is the normal ILS rate
Keep 500 fpm; it will meet the path later
Leave it until the middle marker
steps.why: The rate must match the groundspeed [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]; avoid flying below the glide path, where obstacle clearance is not assured [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]].

steps.s: At BLOOD the altimeter reads 2,100 against 1936 on the chart, and the examiner says, "Needles are centered, pressing on."
options: Press on: the needles outrank the altimeter
Descend 160 ft to match the chart value
Switch to the S-LOC line and its MDA
Name it: failed cross-check; verify setting and ID, or go missed
steps.why: The glideslope altitude at the FAF is there to cross-check the altimeters and verify the indications [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]; if they still disagree, change sources or go missed and request a new clearance [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13c]].

steps.s: At 701 with nothing in sight, the examiner keeps descending "to the real DA of 600."
options: Fine: 600 is the DA printed on the line
Level at 650 and look for a few seconds
Name it: misapplied DA; 701 is the DA, go missed now
Continue to 600, then decide
steps.why: The authorized DA is the highest that applies, and the Montgomery note makes it 701 [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]] [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]; with no required reference at the DA, the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].
